title: Who Counts?
sub: Grades 5–8 · Math · Percent, ratio and the median of a monument count
objective: Students use the numbers in the exhibition’s *Who Gets Remembered?* room, from Monument Lab’s National Monument Audit (2021), to test poster 1’s claim that women’s roles have often been overshadowed. They write 3 of 50 as a fraction, decimal and percent, compare with ratios, find the median of the Top 50, and decide which numbers are evidence for the claim and which only sound impressive.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Numbers are how a claim that women have been overlooked stops being an opinion and becomes something we can check. Knowing which numbers count as evidence, and which only sound impressive, is a skill for every news story you will read.

materials: *Who Gets Remembered?* on a screen, or page 3 of this plan
questions: Is 3 out of 50 a lot or a little? Compared with what?
Why might so few women have monuments?
What could a count of monuments never tell you about a person?
Whose stories are missing from the history you learn, and how could we find them?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the posters
connection: **Online,** *Who Gets Remembered?* shows the list with its counts, and *Tip the scale* asks which facts are evidence. **In the exhibition,** poster 1 makes the claim this lesson tests.

steps.title: How many?
script: Open *Who Gets Remembered?* (or read from page 3): *“These are the 50 people with the most public monuments in the United States. How many do you think are women?”* Every student writes a guess and turns it into a percent of 50.

screen.alt: The Who Gets Remembered? room: rows of statue figures, a few of them orange, beside a question and a guess
screen.caption: These are the 50 people with the most public monuments in the United States. How many do you think are women?

steps.purpose: Commit to a guess before seeing the data.
students: What percent of 50 is your guess?

steps.title: Three
script: Reveal: only **three**, Joan of Arc, Harriet Tubman and Sacagawea. Ask: *“Is 3 out of 50 a lot or a little? Compared with what?”* That question is the lesson.

screen.text:
Only 3 of the 50 are women.
Joan of Arc · Harriet Tubman · Sacagawea
screen.cite: Monument Lab, National Monument Audit (2021), in Who Gets Remembered?

steps.purpose: Reveal the answer, and turn it into a question for mathematicians.
students: How far off was your guess?
Is 3 out of 50 a lot or a little? Compared with what?

steps.title: Percent, ratio, median
script: **Percent.** 3 of 50 is 3/50. Scale it to a hundred: 3/50 = 6/100 = 0.06 = **6%**, the figure the room gives. So **47** of the 50, or 94%, are men.

**Ratio.** Among the 48,178 monuments the audit studied, **22** depict mermaids and **2** honor US congresswomen (Barbara Jordan of Texas and Millicent Fenwick of New Jersey). 22 : 2 = 11 : 1: **eleven times as many** monuments to imaginary women as to real women who served in Congress.

**Median.** Fifty counts in order have no single middle; the median is halfway between the 25th and 26th: Tecumseh (21) and Alexander Hamilton (20), so **20.5**. Joan of Arc (26) and Harriet Tubman (21) sit above it; Sacagawea (20), just below.

examples.title: Mermaids and congresswomen
steps: 22 monuments to mermaids; 2 to US congresswomen.

examples.title: The middle of the Top 50
steps: Fifty counts in order: the middle falls between rank 25 (21) and rank 26 (20).

steps.purpose: Meet the three tools of the handouts, each on one of the room’s numbers.

steps.title: The data
script: **The data.** Put up the Top 10 and the three women (page 3). Lincoln alone has **193**; the three women together have 26 + 21 + 20 = **67**. Ask what that comparison does and does not show.

screen.caption: Monuments to the Top 10, and to the three women in the Top 50

steps.purpose: See the counts themselves, and where the three women sit.
students: Lincoln has 193. How many do the three women have together?
Is each woman above or below the median of 20.5?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three use the same numbers from the room.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Shade 3 of 50 and 6 of 100 to see they are equal, write the men as a fraction and a percent, compare the mermaids with the congresswomen, and draw bars for Lincoln and the three women.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Fill a fraction, decimal and percent table from the room’s numbers, compare with ratios, find the median of the Top 50 and place each woman against it, and say what the numbers show.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Work out how many women a Top 50 of half women would hold, decide which numbers are evidence for poster 1’s claim and which are not, compare two ways of graphing the same counts, and write what a count can never show.

steps.purpose: Work the monument numbers at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the room’s own numbers to test a claim.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down; ask a Red Level student to answer the last.

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.

steps.purpose: Check what each student can now do against the objectives.
students: write a part of a whole as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
compare two amounts with a ratio?
find a median, and use it to compare?
judge which numbers are fair evidence, and what a count can’t show?

steps.title: Where you live
script: Close with the room’s question: *“Whose statues, plaques or street names are there where you live? Who chose them?”* How could the class count them, and compare?

screen.question: Whose statues, plaques or street names are there where you live? Who chose them?

steps.purpose: Take the count home: students can collect data of their own.
students: How could you count them? What would you compare?
